newsitem.title: TANZANIA: African leaders discuss lifting Burundi sanctions.
newsitem.headline: African leaders discuss lifting Burundi sanctions.

text.p: African leaders and Burundi's Tutsi military ruler discussed the lifting or easing of sanctions on Burundi on Wednesday at a summit in northern Tanzania.

It was the first regional summit on Burundi attended by Buyoya, who seized power on July 25 last year in a coup by the Tutsi-dominated Burundi army and was welcomed as "president" to Wednesday's summit by host Tanzanian President Benjamin Mkapa.

"There were discussion on whether sanctions should be relaxed or lifted altogether but no decision was made," said a Kenyan official who left the closed door talks with Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi after about two-and-a-half hours.
Officials gave no explanation for why the Kenyan delegation left the talks but Moi was smiling as he walked to his car.
Addressing the leaders at the start of the summit at the Arusha conference centre, Mkapa said: "For us today to focus entirely on reviewing sanctions is to miss the forest for the trees.

"Sanctions were imposed only as a tool for a specific purpose. Sanctions were only intended to open the ears, eyes and minds of all stake-holders in Burundi to avoid the path of mutual annihiliation."
Regional leaders imposed sanctions on landlocked Burundi on July 31 last year, demanding Buyoya return the country to constitutional rule and open unconditional talks with rebels.
Buyoya has said he is ready for unconditional talks but has not begun them. Negotiations are opposed by hardline members of the Tutsi-dominated army and former military ruler Jean-Baptiste Bagaza.
In his opening speech, Mkapa referred three times to "President Buyoya", who briefed the leaders on the political situation in Burundi and steps towards meeting their demands.

The summit was attended by Mkapa, Moi, the prime ministers of Rwanda and Ethiopia, Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, Zambian President Frederick Chiluba, Organisation of African Unity Secretary-General Salim Ahmed Salim and former Tanzanian president Julius Nyerere, international mediator on Burundi.
Buyoya, a Tutsi, and the army ousted Burundi's civilian Hutu president in the coup last year but says the sanctions only hurt the poorest and are fuelling Tutsi extremism in the country.
But in his latest report, U.N. Special Rapporteur for Human Rights Paulo Pinheiro said in February "there is no sign of the beginnings of a Burundi strategy for peace and reconciliation".
The report added that while the government said it wanted to hold talks with all parties to the conflict "it's actual political decisions seem, on the contrary, to be war-oriented".
More than 150,000 people have been killed in massacres and fighting between the army and rebels since the killing of Burundi's first elected Hutu president Melchior Ndadaye in October 1993.
Hutu rebels led by former Burundi minister Leonard Nyangoma took issue with Buyoya's trip to Tanzania, saying he had not met conditions set by the heads of state for sanctions to be lifted.
Preliminary findings of a U.N.-funded independent study of the sanctions issued on Tuesday found no hard evidence they had succeeded in political aims while smuggling was weakening their impact.

"While it is possible that concessions by the regime may, in part, be the result of prolonged sanctions, there is no concrete evidence that sanctions have been (politically) successful," said researchers from Brown University in the United States.
They suggested sanctions should be retargeted to protect the vulnerable and more items should be exempted for aid agencies.
